headings.title: Introduction and Anatomical Pathway
headings.content: Pulmonary circulation is the movement of blood from the heart to the lungs and back again. Its primary goal is simple: pick up oxygen and drop off carbon dioxide. Unlike the systemic circulation that feeds every tissue in the body, the pulmonary system deals exclusively with the lungs. Deoxygenated blood leaves the right side of the heart, travels through the pulmonary trunk and arteries, enters the lung capillaries for gas exchange, and returns via the pulmonary veins to the left side of the heart.

headings.title: Anatomy of Pulmonary Vessels
headings.content: The structural design of the pulmonary vessels differs significantly from systemic vessels. The pulmonary artery is short, wide, and has a thin wall because it operates under much lower pressure than the aorta. These vessels branch extensively, following the bronchial tree until they form a dense network of capillaries surrounding the alveoli. A common misconception is that all arteries carry oxygenated blood; the pulmonary artery is a notable exception, carrying dark, deoxygenated blood away from the heart.

headings.title: Gas Exchange at the Alveolar-Capillary Membrane
headings.content: Gas exchange occurs across the ultra-thin alveolar-capillary membrane. This membrane consists of the alveolar epithelium, the capillary endothelium, and their fused basement membranes. Oxygen diffuses passively from the alveoli into the blood down its partial pressure gradient, while carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction. Any fluid buildup in the interstitial space, such as in pulmonary edema, widens this diffusion distance and impairs gas transfer.

headings.title: Return of Blood and Systemic Distribution
headings.content: Once the blood is oxygenated in the lung capillaries, it gathers into venules and eventually forms the four pulmonary veins—two from each lung. These veins empty directly into the left atrium. Just like the pulmonary artery breaks the rule of arteries, the pulmonary veins break the rule of veins by carrying bright red, oxygen-rich blood back to the heart so it can be pumped out to the rest of the body through the aorta.

headings.title: Hemodynamics and Pressure Regulation
headings.content:
- **Low Resistance**: The pulmonary vascular bed offers very little resistance to blood flow, keeping blood pressure low.
- **Hypoxic Vasoconstriction**: Unlike systemic blood vessels that dilate when oxygen is low, pulmonary arterioles constrict in the presence of hypoxia to redirect blood to better-ventilated alveoli.
- **Mean Arterial Pressure**: Normal mean pulmonary arterial pressure is about 15 mmHg, compared to around 93 mmHg in the systemic circulation.

headings.title: Clinical Disorders of Pulmonary Circulation
headings.content:
Pathologies affecting the pulmonary circulation can lead to serious cardiovascular and respiratory compromise. 
1. **Pulmonary Embolism**: A blood clot, fat, or air bubble travels from the systemic veins and lodges in the pulmonary arterial tree, causing acute ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
2. **Pulmonary Hypertension**: Chronic elevation of pressure within the pulmonary arteries increases the workload of the right ventricle, eventually leading to right-sided heart failure, known as cor pulmonale.
